title: Determinants, Inverse and Linear Equations
summary: Every square matrix has a number attached to it, its determinant, which decides whether the matrix has an inverse. This chapter covers evaluating determinants, their properties, minors, cofactors, adjoint and inverse, solving systems of linear equations by the matrix method and Cramer's rule, and the Leontief input–output model for two industries.

notes.heading: Determinant of a square matrix
notes.html:
The determinant of a square matrix A, written |A| or det A, is a single number computed from its elements.

Order 2:

|ab|
|cd|

= ad − bc. Example: |3 −2; 4 5| = 15 − (−8) = 23.

Order 3 (expansion along the first row): |A| = a11(a22a33 − a23a32) − a12(a21a33 − a23a31) + a13(a21a32 − a22a31). The signs follow the chessboard pattern + − + / − + − / + − +. We may expand along any row or column — choose one with zeros.

A square matrix is singular if |A| = 0 and non-singular if |A| ≠ 0.

notes.heading: Properties of determinants
notes.html:
1. |A′| = |A| (rows and columns can be interchanged).
  2. Interchanging two rows (or columns) changes the sign of the determinant.
  3. If two rows (or columns) are identical or proportional, the determinant is 0.
  4. Multiplying one row (or column) by k multiplies the determinant by k. Hence for an n × n matrix, |kA| = kn|A|.
  5. If each element of a row is a sum of two terms, the determinant splits into a sum of two determinants.
  6. Adding a multiple of one row (column) to another row (column) does not change the determinant: Ri → Ri + kRj.
  7. |AB| = |A| |B|; |A−1| = 1/|A|; for an n × n matrix, |adj A| = |A|n − 1.

notes.heading: Minors, cofactors, adjoint and inverse
notes.html:
• Minor Mij: the determinant left after deleting the i-th row and j-th column.
  • Cofactor Aij = (−1)i + j Mij.
  • Sum of products of the elements of a row with their own cofactors = |A|; with the cofactors of another row = 0.
  • Adjoint adj A = transpose of the matrix of cofactors.
  • A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I.
  • Inverse: if |A| ≠ 0, A−1 = (1/|A|) adj A, and AA−1 = A−1A = I. A singular matrix has no inverse.
  • For a 2 × 2 matrix with rows (a, b), (c, d): A−1 = 1/(ad − bc) × [rows (d, −b), (−c, a)] — swap the diagonal, change the sign of the other two.
  • (AB)−1 = B−1A−1; (A′)−1 = (A−1)′.

notes.heading: Solving linear equations: matrix method and Cramer's rule
notes.html:
A system such as a1x + b1y + c1z = d1, … is written AX = B, with A the coefficient matrix, X the column of unknowns and B the column of constants.

  • Matrix method: if |A| ≠ 0, the system has the unique solution X = A−1B (consistent).
  • If |A| = 0, find (adj A)B: if (adj A)B ≠ O the system is inconsistent (no solution); if (adj A)B = O it has infinitely many solutions or none (check further).
  • Cramer's rule: let D = |A| and let Dx, Dy, Dz be the determinants obtained by replacing the x-, y-, z-column of A by the column B. If D ≠ 0, x = Dx/D, y = Dy/D, z = Dz/D.
  • If D = 0 and at least one of Dx, Dy, Dz ≠ 0, the system is inconsistent.

notes.heading: Leontief input–output model (two industries)
notes.html:
In an economy with two industries, each industry uses part of its own output and part of the other's output as inputs; the rest meets final (external) demand. If aij = value of input from industry i needed to produce ₹1 of output of industry j, the technology (input–output coefficient) matrix is A = [aij], with aij = (amount supplied by i to j)/(total output of j).

Balance equation: total output = inter-industry use + final demand, i.e. X = AX + D, so (I − A)X = D and X = (I − A)−1D.

Hawkins–Simon conditions (system is viable, i.e. can meet any positive final demand): the diagonal elements of I − A are positive and |I − A| > 0.

Worked Example 3. A = rows (0.2, 0.3), (0.4, 0.1); final demand D = (60, 90) (₹ crore). Find the total outputs.

I − A = rows (0.8, −0.3), (−0.4, 0.9). Diagonal elements 0.8, 0.9 > 0 and |I − A| = 0.72 − 0.12 = 0.60 > 0, so the system is viable.

(I − A)−1 = (1/0.6) × rows (0.9, 0.3), (0.4, 0.8).

X1 = (0.9 × 60 + 0.3 × 90)/0.6 = (54 + 27)/0.6 = 135; X2 = (0.4 × 60 + 0.8 × 90)/0.6 = (24 + 72)/0.6 = 160.

Check: industry 1: 0.2(135) + 0.3(160) + 60 = 27 + 48 + 60 = 135 ✓.

notes.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
notes.html:
• Forgetting the alternating signs (−1)i + j when finding cofactors, or forgetting to transpose the cofactor matrix to get adj A.
  • Writing |kA| = k|A|; for an n × n matrix it is kn|A|.
  • Using X = BA−1 instead of X = A−1B.
  • In Cramer's rule replacing a row instead of a column by the constants.
  • In Leontief problems dividing by the output of the supplying industry; aij is divided by the total output of the using industry j (the column industry).
  • Concluding "infinitely many solutions" just because |A| = 0 — first check (adj A)B.

mcqs.q: Which technology matrix (rows given) does NOT satisfy the Hawkins–Simon conditions?

Assertion (A): The matrix with rows (2, 4), (3, 6) has no inverse.
Reason (R): A−1 = (adj A)/|A| exists only when |A| ≠ 0.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: |A| = 12 − 12 = 0, so A is singular. A is true precisely because of R.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Interchanging two rows of a determinant leaves its value unchanged.
Reason (R): The value of a determinant is unchanged when it is transposed.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Interchanging two rows changes the sign, so A is false. R (|A′| = |A|) is true.

questions.q: Without expanding, show that the determinant with rows (1, a, b + c), (1, b, c + a), (1, c, a + b) is zero.
questions.answerHtml:
Apply C3 → C3 + C2. The third column becomes (a + b + c, a + b + c, a + b + c).

Take (a + b + c) common from C3: the determinant = (a + b + c) × |1 a 1; 1 b 1; 1 c 1|.

Now C1 and C3 are identical, so the determinant is 0. Hence the given determinant = 0.

questions.q: In a two-industry economy the technology matrix A has rows (0.2, 0.3), (0.4, 0.1). Check the Hawkins–Simon conditions and find the gross outputs needed to meet final demands of 60 and 90 (₹ crore).
questions.answerHtml:
I − A has rows (0.8, −0.3), (−0.4, 0.9). Diagonal entries 0.8 and 0.9 are positive; |I − A| = 0.72 − 0.12 = 0.60 > 0. Both conditions hold — the system is viable.

(I − A)−1 = (1/0.6) × rows (0.9, 0.3), (0.4, 0.8).

X1 = (0.9 × 60 + 0.3 × 90)/0.6 = 81/0.6 = 135; X2 = (0.4 × 60 + 0.8 × 90)/0.6 = 96/0.6 = 160.

Gross outputs: ₹135 crore and ₹160 crore.

questions.q: Using the matrix method, solve: x + y + z = 6, 2x − y + z = 3, x + 2y − z = 2.

Case study. An economy has two sectors, Agriculture (A) and Industry (I). The inter-sector flows (₹ crore) are:
Agriculture: supplies 40 to A, 90 to I; final demand 70; total output 200.
Industry: supplies 60 to A, 60 to I; final demand 180; total output 300.
(i) Find the technology matrix.
(ii) Verify the Hawkins–Simon conditions.
(iii) Find the total outputs needed if final demands change to 110 (A) and 220 (I).
questions.answerHtml:
Supplier \ UserAgricultureIndustryFinal demandTotal output
Agriculture409070200
Industry6060180300

(i) Divide each column by the total output of the using sector: a11 = 40/200 = 0.2, a21 = 60/200 = 0.3, a12 = 90/300 = 0.3, a22 = 60/300 = 0.2. A has rows (0.2, 0.3), (0.3, 0.2).

(ii) I − A has rows (0.8, −0.3), (−0.3, 0.8): diagonal entries positive, |I − A| = 0.64 − 0.09 = 0.55 > 0. Conditions satisfied.

(iii) (I − A)−1 = (1/0.55) × rows (0.8, 0.3), (0.3, 0.8).

X1 = (0.8 × 110 + 0.3 × 220)/0.55 = (88 + 66)/0.55 = 154/0.55 = 280; X2 = (0.3 × 110 + 0.8 × 220)/0.55 = (33 + 176)/0.55 = 209/0.55 = 380.

Check: 0.2(280) + 0.3(380) + 110 = 56 + 114 + 110 = 280 ✓. Agriculture must produce ₹280 crore and Industry ₹380 crore.
